To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Precambrian shields are composed of two distinct geological elements, the greenstone belts, which are the earliest Precambrian rocks and which form a stable nucleus, and the mobile belts which are the youngest Precambrian rocks, and which encircle the cratons.

the greenstone belts in the early Precambrians of southern Africa and elsewhere are: (1) highly distinctive, (2) world-wide in distribution, (3) of a very ancient origin, and (4) are the product of a distinctive and highly specific geotectonic environment.

The greenstone belts of the Early Precambrian cratons of Southern Africa are of world-wide uniformity in their stratigraphy, structure and metamorphism; they have a characteristic pattern of association with their surrounding granitic terrains; and the greenstone belts were formed in an ancient cratonic nucleus which has remained stable throughout Precambrian time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the ancient, stable cratonic nuclei and the highly metamorphosed, granitized mobile belts which surround and enclose them.
the evolution of the early Precmbrian granite-greenstone terrains, and the mobile belts, and the relationships which exist between them.
the elucidation and understanding of the fundamental elements of Precambrian geotectonics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the light of present knowledge, the early Precambrians of the crystalline shield areas were not, in fact, stable cratons but were highly dynamic and mobile belts.

the Precambrian mobile belts are a highly distinctive and unique geological phenomenon, and that the early Precambrians, as represented by the greenstone belt terrains, are a highly distinctive geological feature which is world-wide in its distribution and occurrence.

the early Precambria was not the product of a single event but was a period of prolonged and varied geological evolution which has resulted in a highly distinctive and uniform pattern of geological events, features, and relationships which are repeated in many parts of the world.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the early Precambian shields were not formed by the amalgamation of small, scattered nuclei.

the greenstone belt terrains of the Precambrian shields are the oldest, and probably the most ancient, of all known geological terrains, and that they have evolved in a manner which is totally different from that of the younger, mobile, Alpine-type belts.

, although there is a world-wide uniformity in the pattern of the early Precumbrian granite-greenstone terrain, there is a marked diversity in the evolution of the Precambrian mobile belts which traverse the shield areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the greenstone belts of the ancient crystalline shield areas of Southern Africa are not only highly distinctive, but also are very similar to those of other shields.
the greenstone belts of the early Precamprian are not to be regarded as a special class of geological feature, but rather as a normal and expected component of the early Precambrain.

the greenstone belts of the early Precamprian shields are not merely a “backwash” of the orogenic events which affected the mobile belts; rather, they represent the earliest, most stable and fundamental building blocks of the shields.
